title: All will forget
hook: soon you'll forget everything, and soon everything will forget you (Meditations 7.21)

segments.voice: Yesterday: keep your color, the emerald that stays green whatever anyone does. Your line was keep my color. Did you stay in your own shade? Day five hundred eighty-nine.

Can you name all four of your great-grandparents? Most people can't. Maybe one name, maybe a story about a farm or a ship. These were people with whole lives: first loves, embarrassments, opinions about the neighbors, worries about what people thought of them. Every one of those worries is gone now, and so is almost everyone who could have remembered them. That might be the most comforting fact you'll hear today. Marcus Aurelius thought so too, and he wrote it down in one short line.

First, the line. Meditations seven, twenty-one, in George Long's translation, is just this: "Near is thy forgetfulness of all things; and near the forgetfulness of thee by all." Two forgettings, facing each other. Soon you'll forget everything. Soon everything will forget you. Second, who wrote it. This is a man whose face was on every coin in the empire. Statues of him stood in cities across three continents. If anyone could hope to be remembered, it was Marcus. And he's right, in a way. We still know his name. But the people he worried about impressing, the senators, the courtiers, the crowd, nobody remembers what they thought of him on any given Tuesday. Third, what it's for. Marcus uses this line as medicine for one particular sickness: worry about reputation. He comes back to it again and again in the Meditations. What will they think. What will they say about me. Marcus's answer is not that people's opinions don't exist. It's that they're brief. The ones who praise you will be forgotten, and so will the ones who mock you. A worry built on something that short shouldn't get to run your whole day. Fourth, the freedom in it. Once you really believe your embarrassments will be forgotten, a lot of fear drains away. The awkward thing you said in the meeting. The post that didn't land. The question you were afraid to ask. They'll vanish, like your great-grandparents' worries. What's left is whether you did good while you were here.
screen: `TWO FORGETTINGS, FACE TO FACE.` · `EVEN THE EMPEROR'S CROWD.` · `MEDICINE FOR REPUTATION WORRY.` · `WHAT'S LEFT: THE GOOD YOU DID.` · then, large: `ALL WILL FORGET.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Bring up one worry about how you look to others. A mistake at work, something you said, a photo, a fear of seeming foolish. Hold it plainly. Now imagine a hundred years from now. Nobody alive remembers it. Not one person. Let the worry sit in that long quiet. Notice what's left when it shrinks. Then let it go, on an out-breath. The bell holds the time.
All will forget. Marcus's two forgettings: soon you forget everything, and soon everything forgets you. Medicine for worrying what people think. Today's word.
Your line: all will forget. The next time you catch yourself worrying how something will look, say the line, and do the honest thing anyway. Day five hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use 7.21 when anxious about reputation, reminding themselves that both praise and embarrassment are soon forgotten, and turning back to what they can do well now.

original.note: Greek: forgetting. In myth, Lethe was the river of forgetfulness in the underworld.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy line about death.
what it means: both praise and embarrassment are brief, so worry about reputation shouldn't run your life.
what a scholar hears: the forgetting of fame is one of the most frequent themes in the Meditations; 7.21 states it in its barest form.

notes: The coin and statue claims are general (Marcus's portraits appeared on imperial coinage and statues throughout the empire); 'three continents' refers to Europe, Asia and Africa within the empire. Confirm framing.
Fame's forgetting as a frequent theme: e.g. 4.19, 4.33, 8.21. Confirm references.
Lethe as the river of forgetfulness: standard mythology.
